To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the range of usable A and J values for the estimation of g(m), as well as the reliability of g(m) estimations, are improved when using curve-fitting techniques to estimate g(m); (2) for the same set of data, g(m) estimates differ between the three curve-fitting variants by approximately 15%; (3) a 15% difference in g(m) can also arise from a stoichiometric error in the estimation of the electron transport-l

(1) the existing methods to estimate g(m) from gas exchange and fluorescence measurements are unreliable; (2) the reliability can be improved by using curve-fitting methods that minimise the sum of the squared deviations from the data of either A or J; (3) the reliability can further be improved by using a stoichiometric factor of 1.2 to 1.3 instead of 1.0 to convert J into A.

(1) the existing approaches to estimate g(m) by analysis of combined chlorophyll fluorescence and gas exchange measurements are not very robust to measurement noise; (2) the proposed curve-fitting approaches are less sensitive to measurement noise; but (3) the proposed approaches are also sensitive to uncertainties in the stoichiometry of electron transport-limited linear photosynthesis; and (4) the proposed curve fitting approaches are based on physiological principles that are different from those underlying the existing approaches.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reliability of g(m) estimations from gas exchange and chloropyll fluorescence measurements.

the question of whether it is possible to improve the reliability of g(m) estimates by using curve-fitting techniques to minimise the sum of model deviations from the measured data for A and/or for J, and whether the reliability of the estimates depends on the choice of the curve-fitting method.
the theoretical aspects of estimating g(m).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no 'best' method to estimate g(m) from combined gas exchange and fluorescence measurements.
there is a large degree of uncertainty when g(m) values are calculated using combined gas exchange and fluorescence measurements.
the existing methods are unreliable for estimating g(m) when g(m) > 0.1 cm s(-1) and that the three proposed variants are more reliable but still unreliable when g(m) exceeds 0.2 cm s(-1).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in order to obtain reliable estimates of g(m), it is necessary to minimise the measurement errors in A and J, to minimise the stoichiometric uncertainty of linear electron transport limited photosynthesis, and to use curve-fitting approaches, which allow a wide range of data to be used.
a reliable estimation of g(m), which is independent of the method used, is only possible when g(m) values are low.

, for the existing approaches, the estimation of g(m), when using the data set generated in this work, would have been unreliable because of their narrow range of usable data, and the estimates would have been biased by 30%.
The main takeaway from our work is that

it is not sufficient to simply use one of the existing approaches to estimate g(m); rather, the user should be aware of the potential problems of these methods and choose the method variant most suitable for the specific purpose.
the range of usable g(m) values should be extended and that the estimation should be performed using a method variant that is less sensitive to measurement noise.
it is not possible to reliably estimate g(m) using combined gas exchange and fluorescence data.
